Diogenes of Sinope. Around four hundred and twelve to three hundred and twenty-three BCE. He was a Greek philosopher who founded Cynicism, a school advocating radical asceticism, defiance of social convention, and virtue as the only good. Living as a vagrant in a barrel and confronting authority without shame, Diogenes made his life itself a philosophical statement against hypocrisy and the illusory values of civilization.

Diogenes was born in Sinope, on the Black Sea. He was exiled and came to Athens around age thirty. He became a student of Antisthenes, the founder of Cynicism, and radicalized the school. He lived in extreme poverty, wearing tattered clothes, sleeping in a barrel or on the street. He used shock and crude behavior—defecating publicly, urinating on people, lewdness—to provoke reflection and undermine social propriety.

For Diogenes, virtue is the only good. Everything else—wealth, health, reputation, pleasure, pity—is indifferent or harmful illusion. He lived according to nature, not convention. Cultural values seemed to him false and enslaving. Freedom, which he called autarkeia, means self-sufficiency. It means needing only what nature provides, unbound by desire or fear. The life of philosophy, he taught, is living poorly and fighting against convention as a kind of spiritual exercise.

He is famous for his encounters with the powerful. When Alexander the Great visited Athens and asked what he could do for Diogenes, the philosopher replied: "Get out of the way. You're blocking the sun." He called himself a cosmopolitan—kosmopolites—no nation or tribe, only humanity. He was pioneering an early vision of universal ethics. He taught by example. His bare life was the message, more powerful than discourse.

Cynics believed civilization corrupts virtue. They advocated return to natural simplicity and radical independence. Shamelessness, they taught, is freedom—refusing to hide bodily functions or obey arbitrary rules. Cynicism influenced Stoicism. Both taught virtue as the only good, but Stoics were more ascetic, less crude. Later Stoics adopted much of Cynicism's ethics while rejecting its shamelessness. Diogenes' fame rests partly on anecdotes, but his core insight endures. Freedom and authenticity may demand radical non-conformity.
